```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = FALSE, warning = FALSE, message = FALSE)
library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)
library(readr)
library(knitr)
library(kableExtra)
```


```{r data}
dengue_sle <- data.frame(
  Country = c(
    "Brazil", "Colombia", "Mexico", "Argentina", "Peru",
    "Puerto Rico", "Cuba", "Dominican Republic", "Costa Rica",
    "Panama", "Honduras", "Nicaragua", "Uruguay", "India", "Indonesia", "Egypt",
    "Thailand", "France", "Spain", "UK", "USA", "China", "Paraguay", 
    "Venezuela", "Ecuador", "Bolivia", "Guatemala", "El Sakvador"
  ),
  Dengue = c(
    1805, 234, 110, 38.7, 113,
    102.6, 280, 17.36, 116,
    433, 157, 81, 0.21, 20.6, 70, 1,
    18.38, 0.5, 0.2, 1, 1.12, 0.61, 451, 
    145, 206, 302.21, 258, 91
  ),
  SLE = c(
    98, 70, 45, 58.6, 40.2,
    159, 150, 100, 70.9,
    80, 68, 71.4, 54.1, 3.2, 37, 6.1,
    85.8, 81.6, 210, 107.14, 72, 37.56, 60, 
    70, 80, 61, 59, 57
  )
)

knitr::kable(
  dengue_sle,
  digits = 2,
  caption = "Dengue and SLE cases per 100,000 (mixed years, conservative inferences)"
)
```

## Scatter Plot

Both axes use a logarithmic scale so that countries with very low and very high values remain visible.

```{r plot, fig.width=10, fig.height=6}
ggplot(dengue_sle, aes(x = Dengue, y = SLE)) +
  geom_point(size = 3, color = "steelblue", alpha = 0.8) +
  geom_text(
    aes(label = Country),
    size = 3,
    vjust = -0.7,
    check_overlap = TRUE
  ) +
 scale_x_log10() +
  scale_y_log10() +
  labs(
    x = "Dengue cases per 100,000 (log scale)",
    y = "SLE cases per 100,000 (log scale)",
    title = "Dengue vs SLE per 100,000",
    subtitle = "Mixed years and metrics — conservative inferences",
    caption = "Data compiled from various sources; interpret with caution."
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

## Spearman Correlation


```{r correlation}
# Calculate Spearman's rho and p-value
spearman_test <- cor.test(dengue_sle$Dengue, dengue_sle$SLE, method = "spearman")

# Format the results into a clean table
cor_results <- data.frame(
  Metric = c("Spearman's Rho ($\rho$)", "P-value"),
  Value = c(round(spearman_test$estimate, 3), format.pval(spearman_test$p.value, digits = 3))
)

knitr::kable(
  cor_results, 
  caption = "Spearman Rank Correlation Results",
  col.names = c("Statistical Metric", "Value")
)
```

## Latin America & Caribbean Subset

The analysis below restricts the dataset to Latin American and Caribbean
countries only. This is the region where dengue is endemic and where the
comparison is epidemiologically meaningful. Non-endemic countries (France,
Spain, UK, USA, China, Egypt, India, Indonesia, Thailand) are excluded because
their reported cases are dominated by travel-associated infections, not local
transmission.

```{r latam-subset}
latam_countries <- c(
  "Brazil", "Colombia", "Mexico", "Argentina", "Peru",
  "Puerto Rico", "Cuba", "Dominican Republic", "Costa Rica",
  "Panama", "Honduras", "Nicaragua", "Uruguay",
  "Paraguay", "Venezuela", "Ecuador", "Bolivia",
  "Guatemala", "El Salvador"
)

dengue_sle_latam <- dengue_sle |>
  filter(Country %in% latam_countries)

knitr::kable(
  dengue_sle_latam,
  digits = 2,
  caption = "Latin America & Caribbean subset: Dengue and SLE cases per 100,000"
)
```

### Scatter Plot — Latin America & Caribbean Only

```{r latam-plot, fig.width=10, fig.height=6}
ggplot(dengue_sle_latam, aes(x = Dengue, y = SLE)) +
  geom_point(size = 3, color = "firebrick", alpha = 0.8) +
  geom_text(
    aes(label = Country),
    size = 3,
    vjust = -0.7,
    check_overlap = TRUE
  ) +
  scale_x_log10() +
  labs(
    x = "Dengue cases per 100,000 (log scale)",
    y = "SLE cases per 100,000 (linear scale)",
    title = "Dengue vs SLE per 100,000 — Latin America & Caribbean",
    subtitle = "Endemic-region subset",
    caption = "Data compiled from various sources; interpret with caution."
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

### Spearman Correlation — Latin America & Caribbean Only

```{r latam-correlation}
spearman_latam <- cor.test(
  dengue_sle_latam$Dengue,
  dengue_sle_latam$SLE,
  method = "spearman"
)

latam_cor_results <- data.frame(
  Metric = c("Spearman's Rho ($\\rho$)", "P-value", "N countries"),
  Value  = c(
    round(spearman_latam$estimate, 3),
    format.pval(spearman_latam$p.value, digits = 3),
    nrow(dengue_sle_latam)
  )
)

knitr::kable(
  latam_cor_results,
  caption = "Spearman Rank Correlation — Latin America & Caribbean subset",
  col.names = c("Statistical Metric", "Value")
)
```

### Interpretation
- **Spearman's Rho (\(\rho\)):** A value close to `1` indicates a strong positive relationship, `-1` indicates a strong negative relationship, and `0` indicates no relationship. 
- **P-value:** If the p-value is less than `0.05`, the correlation is statistically significant. Given the sparse nature of this mixed dataset, a high p-value suggests we cannot rule out that any apparent pattern is due to random chance.


### Notes

- The x-axis and y-axis are both on log scales.

# 1. Summary

Last week I ran the **OBAMA** (Optimization-Based Analysis of Multiple Arrays) tool
on the duck microbiome dataset provided by Dr. Lourdes Peña Castillo. Instead of
using the original `disease.state` grouping (control vs. disease), I regrouped the
samples using the `rfi_group` column from the metadata file, which classifies birds
by **Residual Feed Intake (RFI)** — `A_high` (less feed-efficient) vs. `B_low`
(more feed-efficient). This produces a biologically meaningful comparison for a
feed-efficiency study rather than a disease-status one.

# 2. Files Received

Three files were provided for this analysis:

| File | Contents |
| :--- | :--- |
| `duck_otu_relative_abundance_20.tsv` | Relative abundance table of bacterial genera per sample. Columns: `geo_accession`, `disease.state`, and ~300 `g__*` taxa columns. |
| `duck_otu_presence_absence_20.tsv` | Binary (0/1) presence–absence matrix for the same taxa across the same samples. |
| `duck_metadata_20.tsv` | Sample metadata. Columns: `run_accession`, `sample_alias`, `duck_id`, `segment`, `rfi_group`. |

# 3. Metadata Grouping

The metadata file contains a `rfi_group` column with two levels:

- **`A_high`** — high RFI (less feed-efficient birds)
- **`B_low`** — low RFI (more feed-efficient birds)

All 20 samples are jejunum segment samples. This grouping was used in place of
`disease.state` for the OBAMA run.

# 4. OBAMA MCO Results

The Multi-Criteria Optimization (MCO) module returned **44 taxa distributed across
10 Pareto frontiers**, where frontier 1 represents the most optimal trade-off
between the two performance metrics (Median and Mean relative abundance).

```{r frontier-table}
library(readr)
library(dplyr)
library(knitr)
library(kableExtra)

study1 <- read_csv("Study1 (2).csv", show_col_types = FALSE)

study1 %>%
  arrange(Frontier, Gene) %>%
  kable(
    col.names = c("Taxon (Gene)", "Frontier"),
    caption = "Taxa identified on each Pareto frontier (Study1 MCO output)."
  ) %>%
  kable_styling(bootstrap_options = c("striped", "hover"), full_width = FALSE)
```

<div style="text-align: center;">
  <img src="MCO DUCKS.png" width="600" height="320"/>
</div>

### 4.1 Frontier 1 Taxa

The six taxa on the most optimal frontier are:

```{r frontier1, results='asis'}
study1 %>%
  filter(Frontier == 1) %>%
  pull(Gene) %>%
  paste0("- ", .) %>%
  paste(collapse = "\n") %>%
  cat()
```

# 5. Biological Interpretation

- **Butyrate producers** — *Blautia_A_141781* (frontier 5),
  *Mediterraneibacter_A_155507* (frontier 7), *Faecalibacillus* (frontier 8).
  These Firmicutes are consistently enriched in low-RFI (efficient) birds in
  the literature.
- **Romboutsia is a known RFI-associated genus**. A 2024 study on ducks during    high production period found that RFI "particularly affecting metabolism and    disease-related microorganisms such as *Romboutsia, Enterococcus, and           Megamonas funiformis*" . The fact that Romboutsia_B appears on  Frontier 1 is   a strong validation signal.
- **Lactic acid bacteria** — *Ligilactobacillus* (frontier 4),
  *Bifidobacterium_388775* (frontier 8). Associated with gut health and
  improved energy harvest.
- **Environmental /  noise taxa** — *Bradyrhizobium_503403*,
  *Pelomonas*, *Brevundimonas*, *Acinetobacter*. These appear on the frontier
  but are probably transient gut passengers rather than true residents; their
  appearance is strange and warrants investigation.

The presence of butyrate producers on lower frontiers is the strongest signal
supporting a real feed-efficiency effect in the microbiome.

# Limitation: Missing Sex Data
